body.text: Japan is preparing to adopt a new Defense Industrial Base Strategy by the end of 2026, broadening its defense buildup to address a critical question: whether domestic industry can sustain the Self-Defense Forces through a prolonged conflict.

The initiative comes as Tokyo confronts mounting security challenges involving China, North Korea, and Russia. Russia’s war against Ukraine has demonstrated how quickly sustained fighting consumes ammunition and military equipment.

On November 4, Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro and Economy, Trade, and Industry Minister Akazawa Ryosei met at the Ministry of Defense with representatives of five major defense contractors, including Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and Kawasaki Heavy Industries, alongside Japan’s leading business organizations. Koizumi called for maintaining reserve production capacity for military emergencies and fundamentally rethinking Japan’s defense equipment policies.

The emerging strategy has three priorities: sustaining defense capabilities, adapting to new forms of warfare involving drones and artificial intelligence, and creating a virtuous cycle between defense investment and economic growth.

A central proposal is a government-backed organization linking defense manufacturers with the state. Expected to take the form of an incorporated administrative agency, it would support domestic production, research and development, defense equipment transfers abroad, and startups developing dual-use technologies. The government aims to submit legislation during the ordinary Diet session in 2027, with the new organization potentially beginning operations in fiscal 2027.

Cooperation between the Ministry of Defense and the Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Industry (METI) is significant. Japan’s defense procurement has traditionally centered on established prime contractors. METI’s industrial policy experience could help bring smaller suppliers and civilian technology companies into defense production.
Akazawa emphasized the importance of expanding industrial supply chains and utilizing civilian technologies for defense purposes.

Koizumi has highlighted the government-owned, contractor-operated (GOCO) model, under which the state owns manufacturing facilities while private companies operate them. Such arrangements could preserve production capacity that companies would struggle to maintain commercially during peacetime.

This is not an entirely new legal mechanism. Japan’s 2023 defense production legislation already allows the government to acquire manufacturing facilities and entrust their operation to contractors when other measures cannot secure supplies. The forthcoming strategy could give this mechanism a broader role in preparing for military emergencies.

The central challenge is deciding who pays for production lines that must remain ready even when peacetime orders cannot sustain them. Under GOCO, much of that burden could fall on the government and ultimately taxpayers.
Funding alone, however, does not guarantee readiness. Factories also need skilled workers, critical components, reliable suppliers, and the ability to expand output quickly.

As Koizumi told a Diet committee on May 12, Japan plans to acquire thousands of unmanned systems under SHIELD, its multilayered coastal defense initiative. By comparison, Ukraine plans to produce more than 7 million drones in 2026, while Russia is also targeting millions annually. Although the figures are not directly comparable, they raise a critical question: Can Japan sustain drone operations during prolonged military emergencies without a production system capable of rapidly replacing heavy losses?

A contingency in the Taiwan Strait or around Japan’s southwestern islands could require prolonged operations across considerable maritime distances, putting pressure on ammunition stocks, repairs, and replenishment.

Koizumi also called for developing defense equipment with overseas markets in mind. Foreign orders could help manufacturers sustain larger production runs, lower unit costs, and strengthen supply chains, complementing government support for reserve capacity.

Tokyo has already loosened restrictions on defense exports. In April 2026, Japan removed longstanding restrictions that had generally confined exports of completed defense equipment to five nonlethal categories. That same month, Australia signed contracts for the first three of 11 planned upgraded Mogami-class frigates. Such exports could strengthen industrial ties with partners, although the transfer of lethal weapons abroad remains politically sensitive in Japan.

Exports cannot eliminate the need for publicly financed preparedness. Foreign contracts create delivery obligations of their own, raising questions about how Japan would prioritize overseas customers and its Self-Defense Forces during military emergencies.

The industrial strategy is being developed alongside the Takaichi Sanae administration’s revision of Japan’s three key national security documents. The current defense buildup program allocates about 43 trillion yen ($272 billion) for fiscal years 2023–2027. Reuters reported that the government is considering 70 trillion to 80 trillion yen for fiscal years 2027-2031, although no final decision has been made.
On November 5, Japan’s Finance Ministry warned against financing increased defense spending through new government bonds, underscoring the fiscal constraints facing Tokyo.

Ultimately, Japan must find a sustainable balance between commercial production supported by exports and reserve capacity maintained at public expense. Its strategy will matter most if factories can replenish ammunition, repair equipment, and keep the Self-Defense Forces operating when a crisis outlasts existing stockpiles.
